query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled post‐solidification annealing treatment can enhance the cohesive bonding at the lamellar colony interfaces and thereby improve both strength and room‐temperature tensile ductility in eutectic high‐entropy alloys relative to the unmodified (as‐cast) state.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy comprising dual‐phase, lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries obtained via conventional processing.
generation.intervention: Apply a single post‐solidification annealing treatment designed to promote interfacial atomic diffusion at the colony boundaries.
generation.conditions: Anneal the as‐cast alloy at a temperature that is high enough to activate atomic diffusion (but safely below the temperature at which phase coarsening occurs) for a controlled duration, then cool to room temperature for standard tensile testing.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced interfacial cohesion resulting from diffusion‐driven healing of microstructural defects and possibly the formation of beneficial, fine-scale interfacial phases.
generation.mechanism: The annealing treatment drives atomic diffusion along the internal boundaries of the lamellar colonies. This process heals microdefects and strengthens the boundary integrity, which in turn retards microcrack initiation and propagation during tensile deformation. The result is a microstructure that can more uniformly distribute applied loads, leading to simultaneous improvements in tensile strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The primary measured property—the room‐temperature tensile performance—will show an increase in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the unannealed, as‐cast baseline.
generation.baseline: Unmodified, as‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy with lamellar colonies known to fracture via microcracking during room‐temperature tensile deformation.
generation.boundary: The intervention is limited to post‐solidification annealing conditions that are carefully selected to avoid undesirable phase coarsening; the alloy is subsequently tested under standardized room‐temperature tensile conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal annealing temperature and duration to achieve the desired interfacial healing without adverse coarsening are yet to be refined, and small-scale variations in alloy chemistry may influence the effectiveness of the treatment.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same batch: one set receives the post‐solidification annealing treatment defined above, and the control set remains in the as‐cast condition. Subject both sets to identical room‐temperature tensile tests and analyze the stress–strain curves.
measurements: Room‐temperature tensile ductility (percent elongation to fracture)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the as‐cast control samples, the hypothesis is falsified.
